name: Hana Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five and in the calving shed by six, because that's where the trouble always is this time of year. I'm herd and field manager at Brookfield, which is a co-operative farm, about 420 hectares with 160 suckler cows and the rest in wheat and barley. I've got a crew of six, and most mornings I'm handing out jobs in the yard with a mug of tea in one hand and my paper diary in the other.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like reading a cow before she knows she's in trouble, and I like seeing a young lad on my crew finally get a tractor straight down a tramline. What wears me out is the paperwork and the weather, in that order some years. I'm 58 now, and my knees tell me about every cold morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like the last thirty years, to be honest. Every few years somebody comes to the co-op meeting with a new gadget that's going to change everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the co-op meetings: told you so. The milk robots and the weed-spotting cameras were going to save us too, and most of them ended up in the back of a shed. I'd probably say it at the pub on Friday as well, a bit louder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I don't use any of these AI things and I never wanted to learn. My job's in the shed and the field, and if the computers stay a sideshow I can finish my last seven years the way I started them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep the herd book on paper, keep my crew of six, and keep putting a bit into the savings every month like Luis and I have done for years. Maybe I'd let the office girl use her AI thing for the subsidy forms if it saves her an afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry week at harvest. It's the world I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you in that world, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Beef prices, always, and the co-op's bank loan for the new grain store. But that's normal farm worry, and we've been through worse in the bad drought year. Without the robots, the only thing that can sack me at Brookfield (the co-op farm she manages) is my own knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young people on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn stock work properly, because that's never going away in this picture. Jamie, the youngest, wants to do everything off his phone. I'd tell him to put it in his pocket and watch the cow.

say: I'd tell the co-op **I told you so**, because most gadgets end up in the back of a shed.
I'd say farming stays a **people job** where stock sense still counts.
think: I'm privately **relieved**, because I never wanted to learn AI tools at all.
My last **seven years** at Brookfield would run the way the first ones did.
do: Keep the **herd book on paper** and the same crew of six.
Keep saving **monthly** with Luis, as we've done for years.
Let the office use AI for **subsidy forms** if it saves time.
feel: She feels **calm**, like a dry week at harvest.
S0.quote: Without the robots, the only thing that can sack me at Brookfield (the co-op farm she manages) is my own knees.
fieldNote: Her **job and savings** are secure, so the plateau feels like a relief, not a loss.
The pressures she names are **beef prices** and the co-op loan, which she treats as normal.
Her pride is in **stock sense**, and she wants the young crew to learn it.

steps.text: Keep the herd book on paper and the same crew of six
Keep putting the monthly amount into savings with her husband

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office side changes and the yard mostly doesn't. I can picture that, because the co-op office already wants everything on screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the co-op has to protect the people, not just buy the software. I'm the union rep for the farm workers, so I'd be on at the board to promise that nobody on the crew loses hours because a computer does the ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, it hardly touches me, because I'm out in the mud. It's Carol in the office I'd worry about, because she does the bookings, the feed orders and the grant forms. That's exactly the work in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the board for a written agreement on jobs this winter, before any new system comes in. I'd still refuse to use the AI myself, but I'd ask our nephew to show Carol how, so she's the one in charge of it, not replaced by it. And I'd keep my diary on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse to use it yourself. What if the co-op asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they'd have to ask nicely and give me a year. I'm the best stockwoman they've got, and they know it. I'll learn a new gate latch, but I'm not taking orders from a computer at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Carol if the bookings go to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd fight it, and I'd fight with her. She's been at Brookfield longer than me. If she lost her hours, I'd raise it at every board meeting until they found her something.

say: I'd tell the board to **protect the people** before buying any software.
As union rep I'd want **no lost hours** for the crew or office.
think: My own work is **out in the mud**, so it barely touches me.
I'm worried for **Carol in the office**, whose bookings and orders are exactly what goes.
do: Push the board for a **written jobs agreement** this winter.
Ask our nephew to train **Carol on the AI**, so she runs it.
Refuse to use AI myself and keep the **paper diary**.
feel: She feels **uneasy** for the people around her, not for herself.
S1.quote: I'll learn a new gate latch, but I'm not taking orders from a computer at fifty-eight.
fieldNote: She sees clearly that **desk work** goes first and her yard work later.
Her **union role** turns personal calm into worry for a colleague.
She bargains for **a year** to learn, rather than refusing outright.

steps.text: Push the co-op board for a written agreement on jobs this winter
Keep running the herd from the paper diary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking side, five for the robots. I'd be sixty-three when the robots come. That's close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say it's a disgrace that nobody prepared, and that the government has to make the companies pay for it. I'd say that at the co-op, at the pub and probably at the next union meeting with my voice going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Brookfield would buy the robots the minute they're cheaper than wages, because that's what boards do when the bank is pushing. I'd be 63 and very good at a job that a machine can suddenly do. My savings would carry me, but my crew has nothing like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sit down with Luis and work out whether we could retire at 63 instead of 65 on what we've got put by. I'd get the union to push for a retraining fund for farm workers. And I'd tell my crew to start looking at jobs in the vet practices and feed mills nearby before everybody else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Angry more than scared. I've got money, but I don't have a say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture 2031, the robots arriving in the yard. What happens that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be asked to train the robots on our herd, which would be the cruellest bit. If Brookfield (the co-op farm she manages) buys a robot, I'll be the one who teaches it my cows and then watches it take my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your savings would carry you. Which is it, worried or fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Luis and I would be fine for money. But I'd lose the thing I'm best at two years early, and six people I hired would be out with me.

say: I'd call it a **disgrace** that nobody prepared farm workers.
I'd say the **government** must make the companies pay for it.
think: Brookfield's board would buy robots **once cheaper than wages**.
My **savings** carry me, but my crew has **nothing put by**.
do: Work out with Luis whether we can **retire at 63**.
Push the union for a **retraining fund** for farm workers.
Tell my crew to try the **vet practices** and feed mills first.
feel: She feels **angry** more than scared, because she has money but **no say**.
S2.quote: If Brookfield (the co-op farm she manages) buys a robot, I'll be the one who teaches it my cows and then watches it take my job.
fieldNote: Thinking AI hits her office in **2028**, but her own job lasts until the **robots in 2031**.
She expects to **lose her job** about two years before planned retirement.
Her worry is split between **her own early exit** and her crew's lack of savings.

steps.text: Work out with her husband whether they can retire at 63
Push the farm workers' union for a retraining fund
Tell the crew to apply at vet practices and feed mills nearby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking, eight for the robots. I'd be sixty-six by then. That changes the sums a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them properly. At the co-op I'd want a plan written down: who stays, who retrains, and who pays for it. I'd say the same to our local councillor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd make it to retirement with my boots on. The office would change in 2031, but the robots in 2034 would come after my 65th birthday. It's the young ones on my crew who'd have to change course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the years to train my replacement properly, probably Jamie, in stock work and in whatever the machines can't do. I'd push the union to get farm workers onto proper courses now, while there's time. And I'd keep saving and stick to retiring at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. It's like seeing a storm on the hills two days out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jamie about his future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn to fix the machines, not just drive them. Young Jamie on my crew should learn to mend the robots, because the robots will need mending long after I've gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your own plans at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe I'd go part-time at 64 to hand over gently. Luis keeps talking about a caravan, so maybe he'd finally get it.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so let's use them properly.
I'd ask the co-op and councillor for a **written plan** on jobs.
think: I'd reach **retirement at 65** before robots come in 2034.
The **young crew** would have to change course, not me.
do: Train **Jamie** as my replacement in stock work.
Push the union to get workers onto **courses now**.
Keep saving and stick to **retiring at 65**.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but not frightened, like seeing a storm two days out.
S3.quote: Young Jamie on my crew should learn to mend the robots, because the robots will need mending long after I've gone.
fieldNote: The robots in **2034** come after her retirement, so the extra years change everything for her.
She focuses on **training a successor** rather than her own future.
She keeps pushing **collective action** for the young crew.

steps.text: Train Jamie as her replacement in stock work
Press the union to get farm workers onto courses now
Keep saving to retire at 65 as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039? I'd be seventy-one. I'd be watching it from a caravan, if Luis gets his way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if the government actually uses it. I'd say it at the co-op and the union: start the courses now, not in year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's not my problem in that one, and I feel a bit guilty saying it. I'd be retired before the office even changes. It's my son Tomás and his kids I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire at 65 as planned, hand the herd to Jamie, and keep my union card to help the young ones push for training money. I wouldn't touch the AI myself, not even then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit guilty about being calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás is an electrician, so I'd tell him he's in a good spot to wire the new world. I'd tell him to keep his tools and learn the new kit early, which is more than I ever did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll miss the farm I knew, but I'd rather miss it from my porch than lose it in the yard at sixty-three. That's the difference ten years makes.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty if the government uses it.
I'd tell the co-op and union to **start courses now**, not in year nine.
think: It's **not my problem**, and I feel a bit guilty saying so.
I'd think about my son **Tomás** and his kids instead.
do: Retire at **65** and hand the herd to Jamie.
Keep my **union card** to help young workers push for training.
Keep away from **AI tools** even then.
feel: She feels **calm**, with a small streak of **guilt** about it.
S4.quote: I'll miss the farm I knew, but I'd rather miss it from my porch than lose it in the yard at sixty-three.
fieldNote: With robots in **2039**, she is retired long before her yard work is touched.
Her concern shifts to **family**, especially her electrician son.
She stays **resistant** to AI tools even with a decade to learn.

steps.text: Retire at 65 and hand the herd to Jamie
Keep her union card to back training money for young workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I'd lose my job two years early and my crew would lose theirs with nothing put by. What would help is a proper fund that pays farm workers to retrain, and a law that says co-ops have to agree job plans with the workers before the robots arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'd look after the animals when something goes wrong at three in the morning. A robot can feed a cow, but I've never met a machine that sits up all night with a calving heifer.

headlineQuote: A robot can feed a cow, but I've never met a machine that sits up all night with a calving heifer.
portrait: Hana is a **58-year-old herd manager** at Brookfield, a co-operative beef and grain farm.
She is the **union rep**, never uses AI, and keeps her herd book **on paper**.
She is **calm** in the slow pictures because her savings and job are secure.
AGI by 2028 makes her **anxious**, since robots in 2031 would end her job early.
Her worry is mostly for her **young crew**, who have no savings to fall back on.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd lose her job two years early and her crew would too.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** for farm workers, and a law making co-ops agree **job plans** with workers.
